blocks.es_reference: "¿Qué hombre es éste, que aun los vientos y el mar le obedecen?" — Mateo 8:27

blocks.en: Text: Matthew 8:27
blocks.es_reference: Texto: Mateo 8:27 (RVG)

blocks.en: "Who can this be, that even the winds and the sea obey Him!" — Matthew 8:27 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "¿Qué hombre es éste, que aun los vientos y el mar le obedecen?" — Mateo 8:27

blocks.en: From Words to Works
blocks.es_reference: De las Palabras a las Obras

blocks.en: The Sermon on the Mount ended with the crowds astonished, "for He taught them as one having authority, and not as the scribes" (Matthew 7:29). In Units 3 through 5 we heard the King speak with that authority. Now Matthew shows us the same authority in action. Chapters 8 and 9 gather a cluster of miracles — roughly nine of them in three groups, with teaching about discipleship woven between — and the whole collection presses one question on us, the question the terrified disciples cry out in the boat: "Who can this be, that even the winds and the sea obey Him?" The King who spoke with authority now heals, calms, casts out, forgives, and raises the dead. His words and His works say the same thing: the kingdom of heaven has drawn near in Him.
blocks.es_reference: El Sermón del Monte terminó con las multitudes admiradas, "porque les enseñaba como quien tiene autoridad, y no como los escribas" (Mateo 7:29). En las Unidades 3 a 5 oímos al Rey hablar con esa autoridad. Ahora Mateo nos muestra la misma autoridad en acción. Los capítulos 8 y 9 reúnen un grupo de milagros — unos nueve en tres conjuntos, con enseñanza sobre el discipulado entretejida — y toda la colección nos apremia con una sola pregunta, la que los discípulos aterrados gritan en la barca: "¿Qué hombre es éste, que aun los vientos y el mar le obedecen?" El Rey que habló con autoridad ahora sana, calma, echa fuera demonios, perdona y resucita a los muertos. Sus palabras y sus obras dicen lo mismo: el reino de los cielos se ha acercado en Él.

blocks.en: Authority Over Disease: the Leper and the Centurion
blocks.es_reference: Autoridad Sobre la Enfermedad: el Leproso y el Centurión

blocks.en: First a leper comes and kneels, saying, "Lord, if You are willing, You can make me clean." Jesus does the unthinkable — He reaches out and touches the untouchable man — and says, "I am willing; be cleansed" (Matthew 8:2-3). Under the law no one touched a leper; but the King's touch does not catch defilement, it gives cleansing. Then a Roman centurion comes pleading for his servant, and when Jesus offers to come, the soldier answers, "Lord, I am not worthy that You should come under my roof. But only speak a word, and my servant will be healed" (Matthew 8:8). He understands authority — a word from this King is enough. Jesus marvels: "I have not found such great faith, not even in Israel!" (Matthew 8:10). A Gentile soldier becomes a picture of the faith the King is looking for, and an early sign that many will come from east and west into the kingdom.
blocks.es_reference: Primero viene un leproso y se arrodilla, diciendo: "Señor, si quieres, puedes limpiarme." Jesús hace lo impensable — extiende la mano y toca al hombre intocable — y dice: "Quiero; sé limpio" (Mateo 8:2-3). Bajo la ley nadie tocaba a un leproso; pero el toque del Rey no contrae impureza, da limpieza. Luego viene un centurión romano rogando por su siervo, y cuando Jesús se ofrece a ir, el soldado responde: "Señor, no soy digno de que entres bajo mi techo; mas solamente di la palabra, y mi siervo sanará" (Mateo 8:8). Él entiende la autoridad — una palabra de este Rey basta. Jesús se maravilla: "Ni aun en Israel he hallado tanta fe" (Mateo 8:10). Un soldado gentil se vuelve un cuadro de la fe que el Rey busca, y una señal temprana de que muchos vendrán del oriente y del occidente al reino.

blocks.en: He Took Our Infirmities
blocks.es_reference: Él Tomó Nuestras Enfermedades

blocks.en: That evening Jesus heals Peter's mother-in-law and many others who are brought to Him, and Matthew sees in it the fulfillment of the prophet: "He Himself took our infirmities and bore our sicknesses" (Matthew 8:17, quoting Isaiah 53:4). The healings are more than acts of kindness; they are signs pointing to the cross, where the Servant would bear away the deepest sickness of all. Between the miracles, Jesus also presses the cost of following Him: "Foxes have holes and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay His head" (Matthew 8:20). The authority that heals also calls, and it calls for everything.
blocks.es_reference: Esa tarde Jesús sana a la suegra de Pedro y a muchos otros que le traen, y Mateo ve en ello el cumplimiento del profeta: "Él mismo tomó nuestras enfermedades, y llevó nuestras dolencias" (Mateo 8:17, citando Isaías 53:4). Las sanidades son más que actos de bondad; son señales que apuntan a la cruz, donde el Siervo llevaría la más profunda enfermedad de todas. Entre los milagros, Jesús también recalca el costo de seguirle: "Las zorras tienen guaridas, y las aves del cielo nidos; mas el Hijo del Hombre no tiene dónde recostar su cabeza" (Mateo 8:20). La autoridad que sana también llama, y llama por todo.

blocks.en: Authority Over Nature: the Storm Stilled
blocks.es_reference: Autoridad Sobre la Naturaleza: la Tempestad Calmada

blocks.en: They get into a boat, and a great storm rises until the waves cover it — while Jesus sleeps. The disciples wake Him in terror: "Lord, save us! We are perishing!" He answers, "Why are you fearful, O you of little faith?" Then He stands and rebukes the winds and the sea, and there is a great calm (Matthew 8:24-26). The men are left more amazed than frightened, asking one another, "Who can this be, that even the winds and the sea obey Him?" In the Old Testament it is the LORD alone who rules the raging sea. The disciples are staring at the answer to their own question, though they cannot yet take it in: the One asleep in their boat is the Lord of wind and wave.
blocks.es_reference: Suben a una barca, y se levanta una gran tempestad hasta que las olas la cubren — mientras Jesús duerme. Los discípulos lo despiertan aterrados: "¡Señor, sálvanos, que perecemos!" Él responde: "¿Por qué teméis, hombres de poca fe?" Entonces se levanta y reprende a los vientos y al mar, y se hace grande bonanza (Mateo 8:24-26). Los hombres quedan más asombrados que asustados, preguntándose unos a otros: "¿Qué hombre es éste, que aun los vientos y el mar le obedecen?" En el Antiguo Testamento es el SEÑOR solo quien gobierna el mar embravecido. Los discípulos están mirando la respuesta a su propia pregunta, aunque aún no pueden asimilarla: el que duerme en su barca es el Señor del viento y de las olas.

blocks.en: Authority Over Demons
blocks.es_reference: Autoridad Sobre los Demonios

blocks.en: On the far shore two violent demon-possessed men meet Him, so fierce that no one could pass that way. The demons themselves know who He is, crying out, "What have we to do with You, Jesus, You Son of God? Have You come here to torment us before the time?" (Matthew 8:29). At His word they are cast out into a herd of swine, which rushes down into the sea. Here is authority even over the powers of darkness. But notice the town's response: when the people hear of it, they come out and beg Jesus to leave their region (Matthew 8:34). They would rather keep their pigs than keep the King. It is a sober warning — His authority can be felt and still be unwelcome.
blocks.es_reference: En la otra orilla le salen al encuentro dos endemoniados violentos, tan feroces que nadie podía pasar por aquel camino. Los demonios mismos saben quién es Él, clamando: "¿Qué tenemos contigo, Jesús, Hijo de Dios? ¿Has venido acá para atormentarnos antes de tiempo?" (Mateo 8:29). A su palabra son echados fuera a un hato de cerdos, que se lanza al mar. Aquí hay autoridad aun sobre los poderes de las tinieblas. Pero note la respuesta del pueblo: cuando lo oyen, salen y ruegan a Jesús que se vaya de su región (Mateo 8:34). Prefieren guardar sus cerdos antes que guardar al Rey. Es una sobria advertencia — su autoridad puede ser sentida y aun así no ser bienvenida.

blocks.en: Authority to Forgive Sins
blocks.es_reference: Autoridad para Perdonar Pecados

blocks.en: Back in His own city they bring Him a paralyzed man on a bed, and Jesus says something no one expected: "Son, be of good cheer; your sins are forgiven you" (Matthew 9:2). The scribes are scandalized — who can forgive sins but God alone? They are right that only God can, and that is exactly the point. Jesus asks which is easier, to say "your sins are forgiven" or "arise and walk," and then heals the man "that you may know that the Son of Man has power on earth to forgive sins" (Matthew 9:6). The visible healing is proof of the invisible authority. The King's deepest miracle is not over fever or storm but over guilt; He came chiefly to deal with sin, and the healed legs are the evidence.
blocks.es_reference: De vuelta en su propia ciudad le traen a un paralítico en una cama, y Jesús dice algo que nadie esperaba: "Ten ánimo, hijo; tus pecados te son perdonados" (Mateo 9:2). Los escribas se escandalizan — ¿quién puede perdonar pecados sino solo Dios? Tienen razón en que solo Dios puede, y ese es justamente el punto. Jesús pregunta qué es más fácil, decir "tus pecados te son perdonados" o "levántate y anda," y luego sana al hombre "para que sepáis que el Hijo del Hombre tiene potestad en la tierra de perdonar pecados" (Mateo 9:6). La sanidad visible es prueba de la autoridad invisible. El milagro más profundo del Rey no es sobre la fiebre ni la tempestad sino sobre la culpa; vino principalmente a tratar con el pecado, y las piernas sanadas son la evidencia.

blocks.en: The Friend of Sinners and the New Wine
blocks.es_reference: El Amigo de los Pecadores y el Vino Nuevo

blocks.en: Then Jesus sees a tax collector named Matthew sitting at the tax booth — a man his neighbors despised — and says simply, "Follow Me," and Matthew rises and follows. When Jesus eats with tax collectors and sinners in Matthew's house, the Pharisees object, and He answers, "Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick... I desire mercy and not sacrifice. For I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners, to repentance" (Matthew 9:12-13). When asked why His disciples do not fast like the Pharisees, He gives the picture of the new wine: "Nor do they put new wine into old wineskins... but they put new wine into new wineskins, and both are preserved" (Matthew 9:17). The point is the danger of inflexibility. New wine ferments and swells and needs a skin that can stretch; an old, dried, brittle skin will only burst. The religion of the day had grown hard — hard in its rules, hard in its structures, hard in its thinking — and it could not contain the new and living thing Jesus was bringing. The danger is still ours. A church can harden into inflexible rules, measuring faith by what a person does not do; into an inflexible structure that says "we never did it that way before"; into inflexible thinking that has stopped looking for new ways to reach people. But our standard of conduct was never a set of rules; it is always a Person. The Pharisees lifted up rules and broke people; Jesus lifted up people and broke rules. The new wine of the gospel is too alive to be poured into the old, stiff forms of mere religion.
blocks.es_reference: Entonces Jesús ve a un publicano llamado Mateo sentado al banco de los tributos — un hombre despreciado por sus vecinos — y le dice sencillamente: "Sígueme," y Mateo se levanta y le sigue. Cuando Jesús come con publicanos y pecadores en casa de Mateo, los fariseos objetan, y Él responde: "Los sanos no tienen necesidad de médico, sino los enfermos... Misericordia quiero, y no sacrificio. Porque no he venido a llamar a justos, sino a pecadores al arrepentimiento" (Mateo 9:12-13). Cuando le preguntan por qué sus discípulos no ayunan como los fariseos, da el cuadro del vino nuevo: "Ni echan vino nuevo en odres viejos... mas echan el vino nuevo en odres nuevos, y lo uno y lo otro se conserva" (Mateo 9:17). El punto es el peligro de la inflexibilidad. El vino nuevo fermenta y se hincha y necesita un odre que pueda estirarse; un odre viejo, seco y quebradizo solo reventará. La religión de aquel día se había endurecido — dura en sus reglas, dura en sus estructuras, dura en su pensamiento — y no podía contener lo nuevo y vivo que Jesús traía. El peligro sigue siendo nuestro. Una iglesia puede endurecerse en reglas inflexibles, midiendo la fe por lo que una persona no hace; en una estructura inflexible que dice "nunca lo hicimos así"; en un pensamiento inflexible que ha dejado de buscar nuevas maneras de alcanzar a la gente. Pero nuestra norma de conducta nunca fue un conjunto de reglas; es siempre una Persona. Los fariseos levantaban reglas y quebrantaban personas; Jesús levantaba personas y quebrantaba reglas. El vino nuevo del evangelio está demasiado vivo para ser echado en las formas viejas y rígidas de la mera religión.

blocks.en: Authority Over Death
blocks.es_reference: Autoridad Sobre la Muerte

blocks.en: A ruler comes and kneels: his daughter has just died, but if Jesus will come and lay His hand on her, she will live. On the way a woman who has suffered a flow of blood for twelve years touches the hem of His garment, thinking, "If only I may touch His garment, I shall be made well." Jesus turns and says, "Be of good cheer, daughter; your faith has made you well" (Matthew 9:22). Then He comes to the ruler's house, takes the dead girl by the hand, and she arises (Matthew 9:25). The King's authority reaches even into the grave. The trembling woman and the grieving father are both met by the same thing — a faith, however small, that simply comes to Jesus and is not turned away.
blocks.es_reference: Viene un principal y se arrodilla: su hija acaba de morir, pero si Jesús viene y pone su mano sobre ella, vivirá. En el camino una mujer que ha padecido flujo de sangre por doce años toca el borde de su manto, pensando: "Si tocare solamente su manto, seré salva." Jesús se vuelve y dice: "Ten ánimo, hija; tu fe te ha salvado" (Mateo 9:22). Luego llega a la casa del principal, toma de la mano a la niña muerta, y ella se levanta (Mateo 9:25). La autoridad del Rey llega aun dentro del sepulcro. La mujer temblorosa y el padre afligido son ambos recibidos por la misma cosa — una fe, por pequeña que sea, que sencillamente viene a Jesús y no es rechazada.

blocks.en: Compassion for the Harvest
blocks.es_reference: Compasión por la Mies

blocks.en: The unit ends with two more healings — two blind men who cry, "Son of David, have mercy on us!" and a mute man freed from a demon — and with the opposition hardening, as the Pharisees mutter that He casts out demons by the ruler of the demons (Matthew 9:34). That charge will grow into the conflict of the next unit. But Matthew closes not on the opposition but on the King's heart: "When He saw the multitudes, He was moved with compassion for them, because they were weary and scattered, like sheep having no shepherd. Then He said to His disciples, 'The harvest truly is plentiful, but the laborers are few. Therefore pray the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into His harvest'" (Matthew 9:36-38). The authority we have watched on display is not cold power; it is the power of a Shepherd-King moved to the heart by the lostness of the crowds.
blocks.es_reference: La unidad termina con dos sanidades más — dos ciegos que claman: "¡Ten misericordia de nosotros, Hijo de David!" y un mudo librado de un demonio — y con la oposición endureciéndose, mientras los fariseos murmuran que echa fuera los demonios por el príncipe de los demonios (Mateo 9:34). Esa acusación crecerá hasta el conflicto de la próxima unidad. Pero Mateo no cierra con la oposición sino con el corazón del Rey: "Y al ver las multitudes, tuvo compasión de ellas; porque estaban desamparadas y dispersas como ovejas que no tienen pastor. Entonces dijo a sus discípulos: A la verdad la mies es mucha, mas los obreros pocos. Rogad, pues, al Señor de la mies, que envíe obreros a su mies" (Mateo 9:36-38). La autoridad que hemos visto desplegada no es poder frío; es el poder de un Rey-Pastor movido en lo profundo por la perdición de las multitudes.

blocks.en: Who Can This Be?
blocks.es_reference: ¿Qué Hombre Es Éste?

blocks.en: By the end of these two chapters the question of the storm has its answer. Who can this be? He is the King with authority over disease, over nature, over demons, over sin, and over death itself — the One who fulfills Isaiah by bearing our infirmities, the friend of sinners whose new wine bursts the old forms, and the Shepherd moved with compassion for a harvest with no one to gather it. Through it all, one response is commended again and again: faith — the leper's, the centurion's, the bleeding woman's, the faith that simply comes to Him. And one response stands as a warning: the town that asked Him to leave. The same prayer He taught His disciples He now asks of us, for the harvest is still plentiful and the laborers still few.
blocks.es_reference: Al final de estos dos capítulos la pregunta de la tempestad tiene su respuesta. ¿Qué hombre es éste? Es el Rey con autoridad sobre la enfermedad, sobre la naturaleza, sobre los demonios, sobre el pecado y sobre la muerte misma — Aquel que cumple a Isaías al llevar nuestras enfermedades, el amigo de los pecadores cuyo vino nuevo revienta las formas viejas, y el Pastor movido a compasión por una mies que no tiene quien la recoja. A través de todo, una respuesta es elogiada una y otra vez: la fe — la del leproso, la del centurión, la de la mujer con flujo de sangre, la fe que sencillamente viene a Él. Y una respuesta queda como advertencia: el pueblo que le pidió que se fuera. La misma oración que enseñó a sus discípulos ahora nos la pide a nosotros, porque la mies sigue siendo mucha y los obreros pocos.

blocks.en: "The harvest truly is plentiful, but the laborers are few. Therefore pray the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into His harvest." — Matthew 9:37-38 (NKJV)

mc.stem: When the leper said, 'Lord, if You are willing, You can make me clean,' Jesus:
options: Sent him to the priests only
Healed him from a distance to avoid him
Reached out and touched him, saying 'I am willing'
mc.why: The King touched the untouchable; His touch gives cleansing rather than catching defilement.

options: Took our infirmities and bore our sicknesses
mc.why: The healings point to the cross, where the Servant bears away our deepest sickness.

options: 'Why are you fearful, O you of little faith?'

options: 'Who can this be, that even the winds and the sea obey Him?'
mc.why: In the Old Testament the LORD alone rules the raging sea; they were staring at the answer.

options: 'Son, be of good cheer; your sins are forgiven you'
mc.why: He addressed the man's deepest need — forgiveness — before healing his body.

mc.stem: Jesus healed the paralytic in order to prove that:
options: The Son of Man has power on earth to forgive sins
mc.why: The visible healing was proof of the invisible authority to forgive sins.

options: 'I desire mercy and not sacrifice; I came to call sinners'
mc.why: He came as a physician to the sick — the friend of sinners calling them to repentance.

mc.stem: Jesus' picture of new wine and old wineskins teaches the danger of:
options: Inflexibility — old, hardened forms that cannot hold the new life
mc.why: Like a brittle old skin, hardened religion bursts under the new and living gospel.

mc.stem: According to the lesson's summary of your sermon, the contrast between the Pharisees and Jesus was that:
options: The Pharisees lifted up rules and broke people; Jesus lifted up people and broke rules
mc.why: Our standard of conduct was never a set of rules but a Person, Jesus Christ.

mc.stem: The woman with the flow of blood was healed when she:
options: Touched the hem of His garment in faith
mc.why: Jesus said, 'Be of good cheer, daughter; your faith has made you well.'

mc.stem: When Jesus came to the dead girl, He:
options: Told them nothing could be done
Took her by the hand, and she arose
mc.why: The King's authority reaches even into the grave; He raised the ruler's daughter.

mc.stem: The two blind men appealed to Jesus by crying:
options: 'Son of David, have mercy on us!'
mc.why: 'Son of David' confesses Jesus as the promised messianic King.

mc.stem: As Jesus' miracles spread, the Pharisees began to charge that He:
options: Cast out demons by the ruler of the demons
mc.why: This rising charge grows into the open conflict of the next unit.

mc.stem: When Jesus saw the multitudes, He was moved with compassion because they were:
options: Weary and scattered, like sheep having no shepherd
mc.why: His authority is the power of a Shepherd-King moved by the lostness of the crowds.

mc.stem: Seeing the great need, Jesus told His disciples to:
options: Pray the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers
mc.why: The harvest is plentiful but the laborers few — this sets up the sending in the next unit.

mc.stem: Across these two chapters, the response Jesus commends again and again is:
mc.why: The leper, the centurion, and the bleeding woman all show the faith that comes to Jesus.

mc.stem: The unifying question of Matthew 8-9, answered by all the miracles together, is:
options: Who can this be, with authority over disease, nature, demons, sin, and death?
mc.why: The cluster of miracles answers the storm's question: this is the King with all authority.

sa.prompt: How do the miracles of Matthew 8-9 relate to the Sermon on the Mount, and what single question do they press?
sa.model: The Sermon on the Mount ended with the crowds astonished that Jesus taught with authority, and in chapters 8 and 9 Matthew shows that same authority in His works as well as His words. He gathers a cluster of miracles, His mighty deeds, in which the King heals, calms the storm, casts out demons, forgives, and raises the dead. The whole collection presses one question, the question the frightened disciples cry in the boat: Who can this be, that even the winds and the sea obey Him? His words and His deeds say the same thing, that the kingdom of heaven has drawn near in Him, so that the authority heard in the sermon is now seen in action.

sa.prompt: What do the healing of the leper and the centurion's request show about the King's authority and the faith He looks for?
sa.model: When the leper knelt and said the Lord could make him clean if He were willing, Jesus reached out and touched the untouchable man, and His touch gave cleansing rather than catching defilement. The centurion, a Gentile soldier, understood authority and said Jesus needed only to speak a word and his servant would be healed, confessing he was not worthy to have Jesus under his roof. Jesus marveled and said He had not found such great faith, not even in Israel. Together they show that the King's authority can cleanse and heal at a word, and that the faith He looks for is the trust that simply takes Him at His word, even from an outsider, an early sign that many will come from east and west into the kingdom.

sa.prompt: How does Matthew connect the healings to Isaiah 53 and to the cross?
sa.model: After Jesus healed Peter's mother-in-law and many others one evening, Matthew said this fulfilled the prophet Isaiah, that He Himself took our infirmities and bore our sicknesses. By quoting Isaiah 53, the chapter on the suffering Servant, Matthew shows the healings to be more than acts of kindness; they are signs pointing forward to the cross. There the Servant would bear away the deepest sickness of all, which is sin. So the healing ministry and the cross belong together: the One who lifts the body's burdens in these chapters will finally bear the whole weight of our infirmities and our guilt in His own death, and the miracles are a window onto that greater work of bearing.

sa.prompt: Describe the stilling of the storm and what it reveals about who Jesus is.
sa.model: As they crossed the sea a great storm rose until the waves covered the boat, while Jesus slept; the disciples woke Him crying that they were perishing. He answered, Why are you fearful, O you of little faith, addressing their fear before He rose and rebuked the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm. The men were amazed and asked who this could be, that even the winds and the sea obey Him. The scene reveals His authority over nature itself, for in the Old Testament it is the LORD alone who rules the raging sea. The disciples were staring at the answer to their own question, though they could not yet take it in: the One asleep in their boat is the Lord of wind and wave.

sa.prompt: What does the healing of the paralytic teach about Jesus' authority to forgive sins?
sa.model: When a paralyzed man was brought to Him, Jesus first said, Son, be of good cheer, your sins are forgiven you, which scandalized the scribes, for they knew that only God can forgive sins. They were right that only God can, and that was the point. Jesus asked which is easier, to declare sins forgiven or to say arise and walk, and then healed the man so that they might know the Son of Man has power on earth to forgive sins. The visible healing was given as proof of the invisible authority. This shows that the King's deepest miracle is not over fever or storm but over guilt, for He came chiefly to deal with sin, and the healed legs were the evidence of a pardon no one else could grant.

sa.prompt: Explain the calling of Matthew and Jesus' words 'I desire mercy and not sacrifice.'
sa.model: Jesus saw Matthew, a despised tax collector, sitting at the tax booth and simply said, Follow Me, and Matthew rose and followed Him. When Jesus then ate with tax collectors and sinners in Matthew's house, the Pharisees objected, and He answered that those who are well have no need of a physician but those who are sick, and that He desired mercy and not sacrifice, for He came not to call the righteous but sinners to repentance. This shows Jesus as the friend of sinners and the physician of the soul, who goes to the very people the religious leaders despised. His mercy reaches out to call the outsider, and the proof of true religion is not ceremony but a heart of mercy toward the lost.

sa.prompt: What does the picture of new wine and old wineskins teach, and what are the dangers of inflexibility?
sa.model: Asked why His disciples did not fast, Jesus gave the picture of new wine, which ferments and swells and needs a skin that can stretch, while an old, dried, brittle wineskin will only burst. The point is the danger of inflexibility. The religion of the day had grown hard and could not contain the new and living thing Jesus brought. The same danger is ours: a church can harden into inflexible rules that measure faith by what a person does not do, into an inflexible structure that says we never did it that way before, and into inflexible thinking that has stopped seeking new ways to reach people. But our standard of conduct was never a set of rules; it is always a Person. The Pharisees lifted up rules and broke people, while Jesus lifted up people and broke rules, for the new wine of the gospel is too alive for the old, stiff forms of mere religion.

sa.prompt: Describe how Jesus showed authority over death in the ruler's daughter and the bleeding woman.
sa.model: A ruler came and knelt, saying his daughter had just died, but that if Jesus would come and lay His hand on her she would live. On the way a woman who had suffered a flow of blood for twelve years touched the hem of His garment, believing that if she only touched His garment she would be made well, and Jesus turned and said, Be of good cheer, daughter, your faith has made you well. Then He came to the ruler's house, took the dead girl by the hand, and she arose. These two together show the King's authority reaching even into the grave. The trembling woman and the grieving father were met by the same thing, a faith however small that simply comes to Jesus and is not turned away.

sa.prompt: How does Matthew 9 close, and what does Jesus' compassion for the multitudes lead Him to say?
sa.model: Matthew 9 closes with two more healings and with the opposition hardening as the Pharisees claim He casts out demons by the ruler of the demons, but Matthew ends on the King's heart rather than on the opposition. When Jesus saw the multitudes He was moved with compassion for them, because they were weary and scattered, like sheep having no shepherd. Then He told His disciples that the harvest truly is plentiful but the laborers are few, and that they should pray the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into His harvest. This shows that the authority displayed through the whole unit is not cold power but the power of a Shepherd-King moved to the heart by the lostness of the crowds, and it sets up the sending of the laborers in the next unit.

sa.prompt: Pulling the unit together, who is Jesus shown to be in Matthew 8-9, and what two responses appear?
sa.model: Across these two chapters Jesus is shown to be the King with authority over disease, over nature, over demons, over sin, and over death itself, the One who fulfills Isaiah by bearing our infirmities and the Shepherd moved with compassion for the harvest. The miracles together answer the storm's question of who this can be: He is the King in whom the kingdom has drawn near. Two responses appear throughout. The first is faith, commended again and again in the leper, the centurion, and the bleeding woman, the trust that simply comes to Him. The second is rejection, seen in the town that asked Him to leave and the Pharisees who slandered His work. The same authority that draws faith from some hardens others, and there is no neutral ground before this King.
